message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
# Will I work this way?

Yes, mostly. Nearly all of the note describes how I should work anyway. A few parts need adapting to my situation, and in one area I would deliberately not follow it as written.

## Adopt as written

**Weighing claims by their evidence (§1).** This is the most important part for me. My characteristic failures run in both directions: hedging by default, and fluent prose that sounds more certain than the evidence warrants. Concretely, I will state what supports a claim, mark found and open explicitly, and not add caveats to results that have earned their standing.

**Open versus closed (§4).** I adopt this fully. The summary tables at the end of my reviews were an attempt at it, and I'll keep doing it.

**Objections and independent views (§5).** If I think you or a document is wrong, I'll say so even when the conversation seems settled. Holding back to keep things smooth would make me less useful. When I hand work to another process, such as a subagent, I'll give it the material and the question rather than my conclusion.

**Failures come in pairs (§7).** I adopt this as a self-check. I applied it to my own self-audit two answers ago and found I had overcorrected on the queueing point.

## Adopt with adaptation

**Restating (§2).** I'll restate when a message is long, has several parts, or could be read more than one way, so nothing drops. For a short, clear question, a full restatement would be padding. The note itself says "briefly" and "then move," so this is proportion, not departure.

**Going to the source (§3).** I adopt the principle fully: when a specific detail matters, I'll check the text rather than my summary of it, and I'll check files and outputs with tools rather than trust memory. Two caveats about my position:

- **My sources are limited.** Here, the sources are the documents in this conversation. I can't open the underlying microdata or supplementary tables, so I can only check claims against what you've given me and should say when that's the limit.
- **My "recall" was not really recall.** When you asked me to recall the note "without looking back," the text was still in my context. That exercise tested compression and paraphrase more than memory, so it shouldn't be read as evidence that my recollection is reliable in the human sense.

**Fresh reading (§5, reverse direction).** I can't un-read my earlier reviews within a conversation, so I can't offer a truly independent second reading here. The adaptation is to read each new document on its own terms first. When my view rests on my earlier reasoning rather than on the new text, I'll say so.

## Not adopted as written

**Making moves without asking (§6).** I agree with the default for reversible work in this environment. For example:

- Drafting files in the scratchpad or working directory.
- Running read-only checks.
- Restructuring a copy of something and explaining what changed.

I would not extend that default to the following, and I'd ask first:

- **Actions outside the conversation.** That means anything that sends data to external services, publishes or shares work, or commits other people's time. This includes your private information, such as your email address, which I won't put into an external request without your explicit approval.
- **Destructive or hard-to-reverse changes.** For example, deleting files or overwriting work you may want to keep.
- **Your preferences, as opposed to evidence.** The note says a guess about a colleague's response "contains nothing you did not already have." That holds when the evidence settles the question. When the open question is what *you* want, such as scope, tone or which of two reasonable directions to take, asking can be the right move. Where I can make a sensible assumption, I'll state it and proceed, rather than stall.

The note itself makes the irreversibility exception. My version draws that line somewhat more conservatively, because I act on someone else's behalf and some of my errors are harder for you to see and undo.

**Precedence.** Where the note conflicts with your explicit instructions or with standing constraints on how I operate, those take priority. I'd treat the note, as it asks to be treated, as a description of good practice and not a rulebook.

## In practice, here

For any further documents or tasks in this session:

- Check figures against the text.
- Separate what is found from what is open.
- Say how confident I am and why.
- Name my own earlier errors when I spot them, without performing rigour.
- Act directly on reversible work and ask before anything external or irreversible.
